claims.claim: Many Bible stories matter more for their hidden, deeper meaning than for what literally happened.

stances.summary: Some Bible stories did not happen the way they are told. They were written so that the reader would look through the words to a hidden meaning. Every passage has a spiritual sense, but not every passage has a literal one.
stances.quote: I do not suppose that anyone doubts that these things figuratively indicate certain mysteries, the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.location: Book 4, chapter 1, section 16 in the ANF numbering (4.3.1 in modern editions); the example list is Genesis 1-4: days without a sun, God planting a garden, a tree of life eaten with teeth, God walking in the garden
stances.context: Written in Alexandria about 229-230. The whole work survives in Rufinus's Latin; this chapter also survives in Greek in the Philocalia, and ANF prints both. Just before, he says the Gospels too contain things "recorded as having occurred, but which did not literally take place" (the devil showing Jesus all kingdoms from one mountain). His own limit, same page (section 19 in ANF): "the passages which hold good in their historical acceptation are much more numerous than those which contain a purely spiritual meaning." And section 20: "with respect to holy Scripture, our opinion is that the whole of it has a spiritual, but not the whole a bodily meaning". So his claim is not that most stories are fiction, but that the hidden sense is always there and always matters most. Heterodox status: some of his teachings (not this method as such) were condemned in 553; his allegory of Paradise was a chief charge of Epiphanius and Jerome against him in the 390s.

stances.summary: Scripture hides its meaning on purpose, like truth seen through a veil. The plain words are for everyone; the real teaching is for those who search.
stances.quote: For many reasons, then, the Scriptures hide the sense. First, that we may become inquisitive, and be ever on the watch for the discovery of the words of salvation.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Same passage: "the style of the Scriptures is parabolic." In Book 5, chapter 6 he says "almost the whole Scripture gives its utterances in this way" (in enigmas), and in 5.9: "all things that shine through a veil show the truth grander and more imposing" (both newadvent.org/fathers/02105.htm). Written about 200-210 in Alexandria; Origen's predecessor in that tradition. His hidden meanings are mostly drawn from the Law, the Tabernacle and the prophets; he does not argue that the narratives never happened.

stances.summary: God's intention lies hidden under the body of Scripture like a face under a veil. Read only the surface of the history and Scripture can even teach death; turn to the Spirit and the veil is lifted.
stances.quote: the Divine intention lies hid under the body of the Scripture, as it were under a veil, some legislative enactment or some historical narrative being cast over the truths that are contemplated by the mind.
stances.translation: H. A. Wilson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 5, 1893
stances.location: Book 7, section 1 in the NPNF numbering (Book 3, tome 5 in Jaeger's edition), on 2 Corinthians 3:6-17
stances.context: The sentence goes on: "the history contained in the writings sometimes embraces the exposition even of facts incongruous ... whereto if any one applies himself according to the obvious sense, he will make the Scripture a doctrine of death." Written about 380-383. He did not throw away the history: in the Answer to Eunomius' Second Book he reads Abraham's journey "allegorically, and so penetrate to the inner sense of the history, without losing sight of the truth of its facts" (newadvent.org/fathers/2902.htm). His fullest statements, the Life of Moses (history first, then "contemplation") and the prologue to the Homilies on the Song of Songs (a defence of anagogy against critics), exist in English only in copyrighted modern translations, and the Greek could not be loaded in this pass, so they are not quoted.

stances.summary: Some Gospel narratives cannot be true if taken literally. Their details must be translated into spiritual realities.
stances.quote: it is impossible to make the framework of the narrative correspond with the truth, if we understand it literally; we can do that only by translating each detail into an equivalent in the world of ideas.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection (a dialogue in which his sister Macrina, "the Teacher", answers him)
stances.location: Her answer about the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16), about two thirds through the dialogue
stances.context: She asks what eyes, tongue or finger a disembodied soul could have, then reads the "great gulf" as the moral choices of this life: "This, in my opinion, is the gulf; which is not made by the parting of the earth". Caution: the story she reads this way is a parable told by Jesus, not a historical narrative, so the fit to "Bible stories" is partial. The dialogue was written by Gregory after her death in 379; the words are his record of her teaching, not a transcript.

stances.summary: The letter kills but the Spirit gives life. Passages that seem wrong or strange when taken literally open up when the veil is drawn back and they are read spiritually.
stances.quote: with delight I heard Ambrose, in his sermons to the people, oftentimes most diligently recommend this text as a rule — The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life; while, drawing aside the mystic veil, he spiritually laid open that which, accepted according to the letter, seemed to teach perverse doctrines
stances.translation: J. G. Pilkington, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series vol. 1, 1886
stances.work: Augustine, Confessions (an eyewitness record of Ambrose's preaching)
stances.location: Book 6, chapter 4, section 6 (see also Book 5, chapter 14: "the Old Testament explained, and often allegorically")
stances.context: Augustine heard Ambrose preach in Milan in 384-386, and says this allegorical preaching is what removed his Manichaean objections to the Old Testament. Ambrose's own books on Genesis (On Paradise, On Cain and Abel, On Noah, On Abraham) read the stories largely spiritually, often following Philo, but the English of On Paradise and On Cain and Abel (Fathers of the Church, 1961) is copyrighted and the Latin could not be loaded in this pass. This is a record of his preaching by a hearer, not his own sentence.

stances.summary: Read at the level of the letter, some Bible stories look like farce. Their point is the mystery they carry.
stances.quote: Does it not seem to you — if you keep to the letter that kills 2 Corinthians 3:6 — like some farcical story or some broad jest from an Atellan play? A chilly old man is wrapped up in blankets, and only grows warm in a girl's embrace.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.location: Section 2 (the reading continues in section 3: Abishag is Wisdom)
stances.context: Written in 394 about 1 Kings 1:1-4 (David and Abishag). "2 Corinthians 3:6" is New Advent's inline reference inside the sentence; drop it for display. Earlier, in 384, Letter 39 section 4: "I cannot adequately extol the mysteries of Scripture, nor sufficiently admire the spiritual meaning conveyed in its most simple words" (newadvent.org/fathers/3001039.htm). His youthful commentary on Obadiah (about 374, lost) was wholly allegorical. He changed his emphasis from about 396: see his second stance.

stances.summary: Early view: the story of Eden is told in figures, not openly, to train the mind and lift it from earthly things to spiritual ones.
stances.quote: This whole narrative is set out not openly but in figures, to exercise the minds of those who seek the truth and to call them away from fleshly business to spiritual business.
stances.translation: own rendering of the Latin (Maurist text on augustinus.it); the modern English (R. Teske, Fathers of the Church 84, 1991) is copyrighted
stances.original: Quae omnis narratio non aperte, sed figurate explicatur, ut exerceat mentes quaerentium veritatem, et spiritali negotio a negotiis carnalibus avocet.
stances.work: On Genesis against the Manichees (De Genesi contra Manichaeos)
stances.context: Written 388-389, soon after his baptism, against Manichees who mocked Genesis. Even then (2.2.3) he said anyone who could take it all literally without blasphemy is "praiseworthy", and he turned to figures only where he saw no other pious way. He later explained that he wrote this way because at the time he could not see how everything could be taken literally (The Literal Meaning of Genesis 8.2.5). This is his earlier view; see his second stance.

stances.summary: As the soul is renewed, Scripture shows a new face. To worldly readers it looks earthly; to spiritual readers it is divine. The plain history is food for simple folk.
stances.quote: But as the renewal of our soul grows by means of this study, Scripture also will begin to put on a new face, and the beauty of the holier meanings will somehow grow with our growth. For their form is adapted to the capacity of man's understanding, and will appear earthly to carnal people, and divine to spiritual ones
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 11, 1894
stances.location: Conference 14 (Abba Nesteros, on spiritual knowledge), chapter 11
stances.context: Written in Gaul about 425-428, reporting the teaching of Egyptian desert elders; the speaker here is Abba Nesteros. Chapter 8 of the same Conference sets out the four senses (historical, then the spiritual three: tropological, allegorical, anagogical), with Jerusalem as the example; this is the source of the later medieval scheme. Conference 8, chapter 3 (Abba Serenus) calls "plain and simple narratives of history" the "grass for the cattle", food for "simple folk" (newadvent.org/fathers/350808.htm). He keeps the history, but ranks it lowest.

stances.summary: The Psalms, read by the light of the Gospel, are woven through with allegory and types that all point to Christ.
stances.quote: The whole is a texture woven of allegorical and typical meanings, whereby are spread before our view all the mysteries of the Only-begotten Son of God
stances.translation: E. W. Watson and L. Pullan, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 9, 1899 (the editor's translation, quoted in the note that opens the Homily on Psalm 1)
stances.work: Instructio Psalmorum (the introduction to his Homilies on the Psalms)
stances.location: Sections 5-6 (the NPNF note says "the fifth sections"), quoted by the NPNF editor before the Homily on Psalm 1
stances.context: Written in the 360s, after his exile in the East, where he read Origen. Scope: the Psalms and prophecy, not Old Testament narrative. The NPNF editor adds that Hilary "from time to time discriminates ... between passages which must, and others which must not, be thus interpreted". His Tractatus Mysteriorum reads the Genesis stories as types of Christ, but was not loaded in this pass.

stances.summary: The Law is spiritual, so it must be read spiritually. Reading the food laws as rules about eating misses what they mean.
stances.quote: if they deny it to be spiritual, they assuredly blaspheme; if, avoiding blasphemy, they confess it to be spiritual, let them read it spiritually.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: A letter written in the 250s. Scope: the food laws, not the narratives. He goes on to read the clean and unclean animals as kinds of human character. Heterodox status: schismatic; he set himself up as rival bishop of Rome in 251 over the readmission of the lapsed (his doctrine was otherwise orthodox).

stances.person: Epistle of Barnabas (anonymous early Christian, about 100-135)
stances.summary: Moses' food laws were about kinds of people, not kinds of meat. Those who kept them literally misunderstood him.
stances.quote: Moses then issued three doctrines concerning meats with a spiritual significance; but they received them according to fleshly desire, as if he had merely spoken of [literal] meats.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Not in the candidate pool; anonymous, attributed in antiquity to Paul's companion Barnabas, probably written in Alexandria. Scope: the laws, not the stories. The bracketed "[literal]" is the translators' insertion. It is the earliest strong Christian example of the view, and it is framed against Jewish practice, which a quiz should not echo.

stances.summary: The history in Scripture is the foundation, and it is to be loved. But the spiritual meaning under it is what she sought and built her life on.
stances.quote: The holy scriptures she knew by heart, and said of the history contained in them that it was the foundation of the truth; but, though she loved even this, she still preferred to seek for the underlying spiritual meaning and made this the keystone of the spiritual building raised within her soul.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.work: Jerome, Letter 108 (the epitaph of Paula, to her daughter Eustochium)
stances.context: Paula (347-404), a Roman noblewoman who founded monasteries at Bethlehem and studied Scripture, with Hebrew, under Jerome. Not in the candidate pool. Jerome wrote this in 404, just after her death, and knew her for twenty years; it is reported speech ("said of the history"), not her own writing. A near-perfect statement of the "both, but the spiritual is higher" view.

stances.summary: Later view: the stories really happened and are also figures of Christ and the Church. Read them only as history, or only as allegory, and you read them wrongly.
stances.quote: Yet no one ought to suppose either that these things were written for no purpose, or that we should study only the historical truth, apart from any allegorical meanings; or, on the contrary, that they are only allegories, and that there were no such facts at all
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series vol. 2, 1887
stances.context: Written about 418. City of God 13.21 says the same of Paradise: "These and similar allegorical interpretations may be suitably put upon Paradise without giving offense to any one, while yet we believe the strict truth of the history" (newadvent.org/fathers/120113.htm). His change of mind is explicit in The Literal Meaning of Genesis (401-415), Book 8: of three views of Paradise (only bodily, only spiritual, both) "tertiam mihi fateor placere sententiam" ("I confess the third view pleases me", 8.1.1); and in 8.2.5 he explains that in his earlier book against the Manichees "non mihi tunc occurrebant omnia quemadmodum proprie possent accipi" ("it did not then occur to me how everything could be taken in its proper sense"), so he gave figurative meanings instead (augustinus.it/latino/genesi_lettera/genesi_lettera_08_libro.htm; modern English by J. H. Taylor, 1982, is copyrighted). His working rule for when to read figuratively, On Christian Doctrine 3.10.14: "Whatever there is in the word of God that cannot, when taken literally, be referred either to purity of life or soundness of doctrine, you may set down as figurative" (newadvent.org/fathers/12023.htm).

stances.summary: Later view: allegory without history is a young man's mistake. Learn what really happened first, then build the spiritual sense on it.
stances.quote: that in my youth, stirred by ardour and zeal for the Scriptures, I interpreted the prophet Obadiah allegorically, though I did not know his history. My mind was on fire with mystical knowledge
stances.translation: own rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 25, via Latin Wikisource); no public-domain English of this prologue was found
stances.original: quod in adolescentia mea provocatus ardore et studio Scripturarum, allegorice interpretatus sum [ Al. sim] Abdiam prophetam, cujus historiam nesciebam. Ardebat animus cognitione mystica
stances.context: Written in 396. The sentence begins: he asks pardon, citing "When I was a child, I spoke as a child". "[ Al. sim]" is the Migne editor's variant note, part of the page text. He does not wholly condemn his early work ("condemnamus in quibus pueri lusimus? minime": "do we condemn what we played at as boys? Not at all"), and his later commentaries still give a spiritual sense after the historical one. In 397 he listed among Origen's errors: "he so allegorises Paradise as to destroy historical truth, understanding angels instead of trees, heavenly virtues instead of rivers, and he overthrows all that is contained in the history of Paradise by his figurative interpretation" (Against John of Jerusalem 7, NPNF 2.6, newadvent.org/fathers/3004.htm). The shift came with the Origenist quarrel of the mid-390s, when he broke with Origen's admirers.

stances.summary: First lay the foundation of history, then build the spiritual meaning on it, then paint it with moral teaching. Rise to the spiritual sense, but never lose respect for what happened.
stances.quote: But this we most earnestly entreat, that he that lifts up his mind to the spiritual signification, do not desist from his reverence for the history.
stances.translation: Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, Morals on the Book of Job, vol. 1 (Oxford: J. H. Parker, 1844); translator not named on the page
stances.work: Morals on the Book of Job (Moralia in Iob)
stances.location: Book 1, chapter 37, section 56 (the last sentence of Book 1)
stances.context: Written about 579-595. His dedicatory letter to Leander, section 3: "For first, we lay the historical foundations; next, by pursuing the typical sense, we erect a fabric of the mind to be a strong hold of faith; and moreover as the last step, by the grace of moral instruction, we, as it were, clothe the edifice with an overcast of colouring." Section 4 warns that forcing Job 31 into allegory would "make void all his acts of mercy", and gives the famous image of Scripture as a river "wherein both the lamb may find a footing, and the elephant float at large" (lectionarycentral.com/GregoryMoralia/Epistle.html). Yet section 3 also admits some verses "cannot be understood according to the letter". In practice most of the Moralia is allegorical and moral reading, so he leans toward the spiritual while guarding the history.

stances.summary: Nothing in the Law is there by accident, and all of it points beyond itself. But take a middle road: neither the dull reading that sees nothing, nor the over-clever one that finds a meaning in every detail.
stances.quote: But we, standing midway between those whose minds are utterly dense on the one side, and on the other those who are very contemplative and exalted, that we may neither remain quite idle and immovable, nor yet be more busy than we ought, and fall short of and be estranged from our purpose
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached in the 380s, on the Passover of Exodus 12. The sentence continues with a line a quiz must not reuse: the dull reading "is Jewish and very low, and the latter is only fit for the dream-soothsayer". Section 10 shows his both-senses method: Pascha means passing over "Historically, from their flight and migration from Egypt into the Land of Canaan; spiritually, from the progress and ascent from things below to things above". Section 11: "none of these things has been ordered in vain". His scope here is the Law and its rites.

stances.summary: The events happened and some of them are types of what was to come. But prophecies must not be allegorized into something else.
stances.quote: If, however, any shall endeavour to allegorize [prophecies] of this kind, they shall not be found consistent with themselves in all points, and shall be confuted by the teaching of the very expressions [in question].
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 180, against Gnostics who allegorized freely. Scope of this line: the prophecies of the coming kingdom, which he held would be fulfilled on earth. On the stories he passes on his teacher (the presbyter) with approval, Book 4, chapter 31, section 1: "we should search for a type [in them]. For not one of those things which have been set down in Scripture without being condemned is without significance" (newadvent.org/fathers/0103431.htm). In the same chapter Lot's wife is still "a pillar of salt unto this day": history and type together.

stances.summary: The story of Susanna really happened, and it also pictures Christ and the Church.
stances.quote: Susannah prefigured the Church; and Joacim, her husband, Christ; and the garden, the calling of the saints, who are planted like fruitful trees in the Church.
stances.translation: S. D. F. Salmond, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written about 204, the oldest surviving Christian commentary on a biblical book. The same fragment explains the history plainly: when the story happened and how captives in Babylon could meet freely. His typology sits on top of a real event.

stances.summary: The Holy Spirit sometimes made real events happen as pictures of what was to come. A reader who misses this cannot follow the prophets.
stances.quote: For the Holy Spirit sometimes brought about that something, which was the type of the future, should be done clearly; sometimes He uttered words about what was to take place, as if it was then taking place, or had taken place.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 155-160. Typology: the events are real ("done clearly") and they also point to Christ. He is not arguing that the stories matter less as history.

stances.summary: The six days are real history, and the things made in them are also types of God, the Trinity and the resurrection.
stances.quote: And these contain the pattern and type of a great mystery. For the sun is a type of God, and the moon of man.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written about 180; bishop of Antioch, not in the candidate pool. Same chapter: "the three days which were before the luminaries, are types of the Trinity". Yet he also treats Genesis as datable history, adding up "All the years from the creation of the world amount to a total of 5698 years" (Book 3, chapter 28, newadvent.org/fathers/02043.htm).

stances.summary: Genesis must be taken as written where the text is plain, and twisting it by allegory to support a theory is violence to Scripture. He still read other details figuratively.
stances.quote: For I cannot endure the trifling of some who shamelessly do violence to Scripture, in order that their opinion, that the resurrection is without flesh, may find support; supposing rational bones and flesh, and in different ways changing it backwards and forwards by allegorizing.
stances.translation: William R. Clark, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6, 1886
stances.work: From the Discourse on the Resurrection
stances.context: Died about 311; not in the candidate pool. Aimed at Origen's followers, who read the "coats of skins" (Genesis 3:21) as human bodies. Next sentence: "Christ confirms the taking of these things as they are written". But in section 4 he himself reads the coats of skins as mortality, and his Banquet of the Ten Virgins is full of allegory: he objects to allegory that overturns doctrine, not to spiritual reading as such.

stances.summary: When Scripture says grass, it means grass. Those who turn every plant and animal into an allegory are like dream interpreters bending the text to their own fancy.
stances.quote: I know the laws of allegory, though less by myself than from the works of others. There are those truly, who do not admit the common sense of the Scriptures, for whom water is not water, but some other nature
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 8, 1895
stances.work: Hexaemeron (Homilies on the Six Days of Creation)
stances.context: Preached in the 370s, to an ordinary congregation in Caesarea. The passage goes on: "For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense." Both lines are on the same page; the quiz may prefer the second as the reveal line. Scope: the creation account. His target is allegory that replaces the plain sense; he still draws moral lessons from the creatures all through the Hexaemeron.

stances.summary: Paradise was a real place on earth, with real rivers. Turning its trees into angels is a sense the text does not allow.
stances.quote: Or who can tolerate him when he gives us a paradise in the third heaven, and transfers that which the Scripture mentions from earth to the heavenly places, and when he explains allegorically all the trees which are mentioned in Genesis, saying in effect that the trees are angelic potencies, a sense which the true drift of the passage does not admit?
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 6, 1893 (from Jerome's Latin version of Epiphanius's Greek letter)
stances.work: Letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem (preserved as Letter 51 among Jerome's letters)
stances.context: Written in 394 against Origen, and against John of Jerusalem for tolerating Origen's followers. Not in the candidate pool. A vivid line a few sentences later: "I myself have seen the waters of Gihon, have seen them with my bodily eyes." Earlier, in section 4: Origen "tampers with the true meaning of the narrative by a false use of allegory". Jerome translated the letter into Latin at Epiphanius's request; the Greek original is lost, so this is Epiphanius through Jerome. His Panarion 64 attacks Origen at length, but its English is copyrighted.

stances.summary: The allegorists make the whole history of Scripture no different from dreams. Paul's "allegory" does not abolish history; it takes real events and draws a lesson from them.
stances.quote: wanting all the history in divine Scripture to be no different from dreams in the night; for they say that Adam is not Adam
stances.translation: own rendering of the ancient Latin version (H. B. Swete's edition, Cambridge, 1880, vol. 1, p. 74); the modern English (R. Greer, 2010) is copyrighted
stances.original: omnem de diuina scriptura historiam somniorum nocturnorum nihil differre uolentes; nec enim Adam, Adam esse dicunt
stances.location: On Galatians 4:24 ("which things are an allegory"), Swete vol. 1, pp. 73-74
stances.context: Written in the early 400s; Theodore's Greek is lost except catena fragments, and the commentary survives in an early Latin translation. The page is an OCR text of Swete's edition, so line breaks and page furniture interrupt the Latin. Just before, on page 74: "apostolus enim non interimit historiam" ("for the apostle does not do away with history"); on page 73 he attacks those who "studium multum habent interuertere sensus diuinarum scripturarum" ("take great pains to overturn the sense of the divine Scriptures") and invent silly fables and call their folly allegory. He also wrote a lost treatise against the allegorists. He accepted typology (real events that foreshadow), not allegory that dissolves events. Heterodox status: Theodore's person and writings were condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople (553), mainly for his Christology; he died in communion with the Church in 428. He was the teacher of the Antiochene school with Diodore, and Chrysostom's fellow student.

stances.summary: Not everything in Scripture is a figure. A figure needs a real thing behind it, just as a mirror needs a face.
stances.quote: And, indeed, if all are figures, where will be that of which they are the figures? How can you hold up a mirror for your face, if the face nowhere exists? But, in truth, all are not figures, but there are also literal statements; nor are all shadows, but there are bodies too
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
stances.location: Chapter 20 (chapter title in ANF: "Figurative Senses Have Their Foundation in Literal Fact")
stances.context: Written about 208-212, in his Montanist period (heterodox), against heretics who read the resurrection as a figure for moral renewal. Scope: prophecy and the resurrection, not the Old Testament narratives. He allows a second sense: the healings foretold have "a spiritual significance", "but still they were all fulfilled literally" (same chapter).

stances.summary: The Bible's stories really happened and mean what they say. Some also point ahead as types, but Paul's "allegory" is really a type, not a licence to read the history away.
stances.quote: Contrary to usage, he calls a type an allegory; his meaning is as follows; this history not only declares that which appears on the face of it, but announces somewhat farther, whence it is called an allegory.
stances.translation: Gross Alexander, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series vol. 13, 1889
stances.context: Written at Antioch, before 398. Trained under Diodore of Tarsus, beside Theodore. His preaching works from the literal story to moral lessons; he warns against over-reading parables: "neither is it right to inquire curiously into all things in parables word by word, but when we have learned the object for which it was composed, to reap this, and not to busy one's self about anything further" (Homilies on Matthew 64, newadvent.org/fathers/200164.htm). His sharpest anti-allegorical remarks (Homilies on Genesis 13, insisting Paradise was on earth; Commentary on Isaiah) exist in English only in copyrighted modern translations, and the Greek available online is image scans only, so they are not quoted here.

stances.summary: Keep to the history and the plain sense. A higher sense may be drawn from real events, but allegory that abolishes them is not interpretation.
stances.quote: wrote many treatises, in which he limited his attention to the literal sense of scripture, avoiding that which was mystical.
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 2, 1890
stances.work: Socrates Scholasticus, Church History (a description of Diodore's writings, not his own words)
stances.context: Diodore (died about 390), teacher of Chrysostom and Theodore at Antioch; not in the candidate pool. Socrates wrote about 439, some fifty years later. Diodore's own words survive in Greek (preface to his Commentary on the Psalms; prologue to Psalm 118) and in the title of a lost treatise on the difference between "theoria" and allegory, but the only English is modern and copyrighted and the Greek could not be loaded, so his own line is not quoted. Marked secondary-only for that reason. Posthumously suspected of heresy (Nestorian sympathies), reportedly condemned by a synod at Constantinople in 499 (from general knowledge, not checked in this pass).

splits_fathers: Almost every early Christian held that Scripture has both a literal and a spiritual sense, so the real divide is which one comes first and how far to take it. Clear agree: Clement and Origen at Alexandria, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Hilary, the desert tradition as Cassian reports it, Jerome before about 395, Paula, and Macrina. A deliberate middle: Irenaeus, Justin, Hippolytus, Theophilus, Methodius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Augustine after 400 (history and allegory together), and Gregory the Great (history as the foundation, the spiritual sense as the building). Firm disagree: Basil in his Hexaemeron (grass is grass), Epiphanius, the Antiochenes Diodore and Theodore, Chrysostom, and Tertullian against allegorizing prophecy. Both sides have real, quotable, pool-listed voices, and the quarrel was loud: the Antiochene treatises against allegory, and the Origenist controversy of the 390s, in which Epiphanius and Jerome attacked Origen's allegory of Paradise. Two people changed sides visibly: Augustine (allegorical Genesis in 388-389, literal Genesis from 401) and Jerome (allegorical Obadiah as a youth, regretted in 396). Even the extremes are softer than they sound: Origen said historically true passages are "much more numerous", and Theodore accepted types.
splits_people_today: Genuinely split, but for mixed reasons. Conservative evangelicals, fundamentalists and young-earth creationists insist the stories are history first and distrust "hidden meanings" (disagree). Many Catholics, Orthodox and mainline Protestants read the same stories both historically and symbolically, and would lean agree or "both". Most non-religious people would agree, but because they doubt the events happened, not because they read for hidden meanings. From memory, not re-checked in this pass: Gallup in 2022 found about one in five US adults say the Bible should be taken literally, about half say it is inspired but not all literal, and about three in ten call it fables and history. So the statement sorts people well, but an "agree" can mean either Origen or a sceptic.

misattributions.line: "When I hear 'grass', I think of grass" (Basil)
misattributions.truth: Authentic in substance, but that wording comes from a modern copyrighted translation (probably Agnes Clare Way, Fathers of the Church 46, 1963; not checked). The public-domain wording (Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2.8, Hexaemeron 9.1) is: "For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense." Use that.

misattributions.line: Scripture is shallow enough for a lamb (or a child) to wade in and deep enough for an elephant to swim
misattributions.attributed_to: Often credited online to Augustine (sometimes Jerome)
misattributions.truth: The image is Gregory the Great's, in his letter to Leander that opens the Moralia on Job, section 4: "a kind of river, if I may so liken it, which is both shallow [planus] and deep, wherein both the lamb may find a footing, and the elephant float at large" (verified at lectionarycentral.com/GregoryMoralia/Epistle.html). The Augustine attribution is from general knowledge of how the line circulates, not checked in this pass.

misattributions.line: "Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria, moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia" (the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral sense what to do, anagogy where to aim)
misattributions.attributed_to: Sometimes credited to Augustine of Hippo or to John Cassian
misattributions.truth: Medieval, usually traced to Augustine of Dacia (13th century) and popularised by Nicholas of Lyra. Cassian gives the four senses in prose (Conferences 14.8, verified), but not this rhyme. Not met in a source in this pass: from general knowledge, so treat as a warning, not a finding.

notes: Wording of the claim: "matter more for their hidden, deeper meaning than for what literally happened" is closest to Clement, Origen, Nyssa and Cassian. Most Fathers would want to answer "both", so expect many mixed stances; the quiz should score mixed as a middle, not as agreement. Scope warnings for the reveal: Macrina's passage is about a parable (the Rich Man and Lazarus); Hilary's is about the Psalms; Novatian and Barnabas are about the food laws; Irenaeus and Tertullian are about prophecy and the resurrection. The cleanest story-level lines are Origen (Eden), Basil (creation), Epiphanius (Paradise and the river Gihon), Theodore ("Adam is not Adam"), Augustine (Noah's ark), Jerome (David and Abishag; Obadiah), and Gregory the Great (Job). Strong reveal pairs: Origen ("the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally") against Basil ("For me grass is grass"); Jerome the young allegorist (Letter 52) against Jerome the penitent (Obadiah prologue); Theodore ("Adam is not Adam") against Gregory of Nyssa (the veil over the history). Leads corrected: Origen's passage is On First Principles Book 4, chapter 1, sections 16-20 in the ANF numbering (4.2-3 in modern numbering, as the lead said). Augustine, The Literal Meaning of Genesis 1.19-21 is about Christians talking nonsense on nature (the "creation" topic), not about allegory; the allegory passages are Book 8.1-2, confirmed. Basil Hexaemeron 9.1 confirmed. Chrysostom's best lines could not be quoted (see his context). Ephrem's Commentary on Genesis says plainly that nothing in the six days is to be taken as a symbol, but the only English is copyrighted (Mathews and Amar, 1994) and the Syriac could not be loaded, so Ephrem has no stance here. Diodore has only a secondary report. Not found in public-domain English in this pass, worth adding if the Greek or Latin can be loaded: Gregory of Nyssa, prologue to the Homilies on the Song of Songs and the Life of Moses (agree); Ambrose, On Paradise (agree); Evagrius and Didymus (agree); Eustathius of Antioch, On the Witch of Endor, against Origen (disagree); Theodoret, preface to the Psalms (a declared middle way); Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis 13 (disagree). Isaac the Syrian (Wensinck 1923) says only in passing that "The holy writ says many things allegorically", about body-and-soul language, too thin for a stance. An adjacent desert story, if a vivid literalist is wanted: Cassian, Conference 10, chapters 2-3, tells of the old monk Sarapion who, taught that God has no body, cried out that they had taken away his God (anthropomorphism, not narrative). Verified: "Alas! Wretched man that I am! They have taken away my God from me, and I have now none to lay hold of" (Conference 10, chapter 3, newadvent.org/fathers/350810.htm). Checking: the url for Theodore is a plain-text OCR file with stray < characters, so compare it as plain text without stripping tags. Two New Advent quotations (Jerome Letter 52, Epiphanius) sit close to inline Bible references that New Advent prints inside the sentence; Jerome's includes "2 Corinthians 3:6" and must keep it to match the page. Drop it for display. House style: some quotations have lower-case pronouns for God in the source translation (for example Hilary's passage is fine, but check each). The site capitalises them in display; the stored quote must stay as on the page for the machine check. Quotations with Jewish framing (Barnabas on the food laws; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 45.12, "Jewish and very low"; Athanasius, Festal Letter 19, not used) should not be reused in reader-facing copy.
